summary: Specifies an OSPFv3 interface type tailored for mobile ad hoc networks, derived from the broadcast interface type and using multipoint relays. This is an experimental protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: In a crowd of moving phones, not everybody should shout updates. A few chosen helpers pass messages along. This is an experiment applying that to OSPF.

subtitle: An OSPFv3 interface type for mobile ad hoc networks that uses multipoint relays to cut control traffic.

tldr.problem: OSPFv3 flooding, full topology advertisement and Designated Router adjacency mechanisms do not suit mobile ad hoc networks, where links change often and a transmission reaches only some neighbors.
tldr.mechanism: A new OSPFv3 MANET interface type, derived from the broadcast type, uses multipoint relays (MPRs) selected through Hello packets to reduce flooding, advertised topology and adjacencies.
tldr.outcome: It is an Experimental protocol. OSPFv3 on other interface types, or in areas without MANET interfaces, is unchanged.

today: RFC 5449 is an Experimental RFC, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines the OSPFv3 MANET interface type, and the text states that OSPFv3 on other interface types is unaltered.

sections.title: Why OSPFv3 Needs a MANET Mode
sections.content:
This RFC extends OSPFv3 (RFC 5340) for mobile ad hoc networks (MANETs). It is built on three ideas: flooding-reduction (only some routers retransmit), topology-reduction (only some links are advertised, so LSAs are fewer and smaller) and adjacency-reduction (adjacencies with only a subset of neighbors, for less database synchronization). All three use multipoint relays, a technique developed in OLSR (RFC 3626).

The extension appears as a new interface type, the OSPFv3 MANET interface, derived from the broadcast interface type. Operation on other interface types, or in areas with no MANET interfaces, remains unaltered.
sections.plainLanguage: Ordinary OSPF is chatty, which is fine on wires but wasteful when the network is made of moving radios. This adds a quieter mode for those radios.

sections.title: What Makes a MANET Different
sections.content:
The applicability statement says the MANET interface type fits an area where parts are a MANET with moderate mobility. In MANETs the topology changes often, wireless links vary in quality, and bandwidth is scarce. They are also "semi-broadcast": a router's transmission is received only by a subset of routers, and two routers' transmissions may reach different subsets.

These traits conflict with existing OSPFv3 control-traffic reduction, including Designated Router based adjacency reduction. The MANET interface type does not demand anything of the network. It describes conditions the protocol must tolerate, so it generalizes the other interface types, and a protocol that works over it also works over a broadcast interface.
sections.plainLanguage: Radios that move around can only hear some of their neighbors, and who they can hear keeps changing. So the old way of picking one boss router does not work well.

sections.title: Flooding-MPRs, Path-MPRs and Synch Routers
sections.content:
A Flooding-MPR is a neighbor chosen by router X to retransmit the broadcast packets it receives from X, provided they are not duplicates and the Hop Limit is greater than one. Each router picks a subset of its symmetric 1-hop neighbors so that every router exactly two hops away is reached through them (the coverage criterion, which MUST be satisfied).

A Path-MPR is a neighbor chosen as being on the shortest path from a strict 2-hop neighbor to the chooser. Router-LSAs MUST include links to Path-MPRs and Path-MPR-selectors, reported as point-to-point links, and MAY list others at the cost of larger LSAs.

No Designated Router is elected. Adjacencies MUST be brought up with all neighbors in the MPR set and MPR-selector set. A Synch router brings up adjacencies with all its MANET neighbors, and a network with no Hybrid routers MUST have at least one. A Hybrid router has both MANET and other interface types and MUST select all its MANET neighbors as Path-MPRs.
sections.plainLanguage: Each router picks a few neighbors as messengers who repeat news so it reaches everyone two steps away, and a few others that sit on the best roads. Only those get close, full-detail connections.

sections.title: Hello Packets and the Three TLVs
sections.content:
All extra signaling goes in TLVs inside an Link-Local Signaling (LLS) block appended to Hello packets (RFC 4813). Hellos on MANET interfaces MUST set the L bit in the OSPF Options field. Neighbors in a Hello MUST be ordered: Flooding-MPRs first, then other symmetric 1-hop neighbors, then other 1-hop neighbors.

The FMPR TLV carries a willingness value from 1 to 6 (default WILL_DEFAULT = 3), the number of symmetric neighbors and the number of Flooding-MPRs. The METRIC-MPR TLV advertises link costs, either one per neighbor or a single uniform cost. The PMPR TLV lists neighbor IDs ordered as Path-MPRs, then other adjacent neighbors, then the remaining symmetric neighbors, followed by 16-bit costs, with the default cost 0xFFFF (infinity). Its S bit marks a Synch router. IANA assigned LLS TLV types 3, 4 and 5 to these three.
sections.plainLanguage: Hello messages get extra notes attached: who I picked as my messengers, how much it costs to reach each neighbor, and whether I am willing to help.

sections.title: Flooding, Acknowledgments and Routing
sections.content:
An LSA received on a MANET interface is discarded if it came from a router that is not a symmetric 1-hop neighbor. Otherwise it is installed, and retransmitted on other interface types, and also on MANET interfaces to the multicast address all_SPF_Routers if the sending neighbor is a Flooding-MPR-selector of this router.

Acknowledgments differ from plain OSPF. A router MUST NOT acknowledge an LSA from a non-adjacent neighbor, MUST NOT acknowledge one it will retransmit (the retransmission counts as an implicit acknowledgment), and otherwise MUST send an explicit acknowledgment to all_SPF_Routers. A router that sent an LSA expects acknowledgments from its adjacent neighbors and MUST retransmit if one is missing. Timers and jitter MAY be used to bundle packets.

Neighbors that never become fully adjacent stay in the 2-Way state, but packets from them MUST still be processed. Route computation MUST include links to neighbors in 2-Way or higher.
sections.plainLanguage: Only the chosen messengers repeat the news. If you hear a neighbor repeat it, that counts as a thank-you; otherwise you send a short thank-you note.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says the generic routing threats in RFC 4593 apply to OSPFv3 as before, so the MANET interface type adds no new threats to OSPFv3. However, using wireless links with no infrastructure can make some of those attacks easier. Sniffing, traffic analysis and signal interference only require being within radio range.

Spoofing, falsification, overloading and not forwarding packets are also possible, and the lack of predetermined authority may make forged information easier to pass off. Mobility can widen a threat's consequence zone, while the dynamic topology may shorten its consequence period.
sections.plainLanguage: Radio is easier to listen in on or jam than a cable, so the same old tricks get easier. The new mode does not add brand new kinds of tricks.

fields.name: Willingness
fields.desc: Willingness to flood for others, 1 to 6; default 3.

fields.name: # Sym. Neigh.
fields.desc: Number of symmetric 1-hop neighbors, listed first.

fields.name: # Flood MPR
fields.desc: Number of neighbors chosen as Flooding-MPR.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Cleared on transmission, ignored on reception.
